item.title: Privacy campaigners to ask court to ban sale of Meta AI glasses
item.description:
Privacy campaigners to ask court to ban sale of Meta AI glasses

October 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two Dutch privacy organisations are seeking an injunction against Meta to ban sales of the company’s AI glasses in the Netherlands.

Offlimits and The Firewall argue that the devices, which allow users to film and record scenes that they are viewing through the lenses, breach Dutch criminal laws that protect people from being photographed and filmed without their consent.

Lawyers wrote to Meta two weeks ago demanding they withdraw the glasses from sale in the Netherlands or face legal action, but the deadline passed without a response from the company.

“Offlimits and The Firewall are demanding, by means of this letter of formal notice, that the sale of the Meta glasses in the Netherlands cease,” they wrote.

Several thousand pairs of AI glasses have been bought by Dutch customers since opticians started selling them a year ago, while worldwide more than seven million pairs have been sold.

Several music venues in the Netherlands have banned the devices after a man was caught filming women near the toilets at a festival in August. Campaigners say it is one example of how the glasses have been used to film people secretly in intimate settings such as toilets, changing rooms and sex clubs.

They also raised concerns about the potential for the devices to be used to film young children in sports halls, playgrounds or nurseries.

Drawing a line

“We are drawing a line,” Robbert Hoving, managing director of Offlimits, said. “Hiding a camera in an everyday accessory encourages online behaviour that breaches personal boundaries. Victims of these glasses are already contacting our helpline.”

Offlimits, which campaigns against online abuse and exploitation, especially of children, said it was concerned that the glasses capture images of people who are unaware they are being filmed, including minors.

Although the glasses have an LED light to show when the camera is operating, it is not always clear or visible, the lawyers wrote. “Furthermore, the LED light can easily be covered up, making it invisible to anyone,” they said.

They also pointed out that the footage is stored by Meta and used to train its AI systems, which they argue is also an offence under Dutch law. “Meta gains access to the recordings made with the Meta glasses, even when people appear in the footage who have not given their consent.”

The organisations hope the court will announce a date for a hearing by the end of the week. Dutch News has reached out to Meta for comment.

item.title: Veilig Thuis asks for €70m as domestic abuse reports mount
item.description:
Veilig Thuis asks for €70m as domestic abuse reports mount

October 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

People who report suspected child abuse or domestic violence are waiting an average of 2 months for national domestic violence network Veilig Thuis to act, and the agency itself now says it can no longer guarantee it will pick up every sign of danger in time.

The network of organisations told broadcaster NOS on Tuesday that it needs €70 million from the cabinet over the coming years to take on extra staff and push through reforms.

By law, Veilig Thuis must carry out a safety assessment within 5 working days of receiving a report. Roughly half of reports have missed that deadline in recent years, and some families wait more than 6 months.

“Normally the waiting list gets a little shorter over the summer, but that hasn’t happened this time,” Ida Ouweneel, a board member of the national network, told NOS. Reports usually rise in the autumn, she said. “We can’t get through them. It can’t go on like this.”

All incoming reports are screened, she said, and cases of acute danger skip the waiting list and are dealt with immediately.

Growing backlog
Reports to Veilig Thuis rose 5% to 136,000 last year, according to national statistics office CBS. The agency says it welcomes the greater awareness, but that cases are also becoming more complex.

“Every day when I start up my computer, I see the number of reports getting bigger,” said Colinda Guiljam, who works for Veilig Thuis in Zeeland. “At the start of this year there were just over 30 reports on the waiting list in Zeeland. Now there are almost 400.”

Ouweneel said the backlog is driven by shortages and waiting lists across youth care, which leave vulnerable children without help and lead to more reports. “Our waiting list is a consequence of youth care grinding to a halt,” she said.

Budget debate
The health and youth care inspectorate IGJ has warned about waiting times for years. Criticism grew in May when it emerged that a 6-year-old girl in Stadskanaal had been severely abused despite several reports to the agency, which has said it acted on them immediately.

Mirjam Sterk, the centrist Christian Democrat (CDA) minister responsible for youth care, told NOS she will meet local council executives, local authorities association VNG and Veilig Thuis soon to discuss what is needed. She did not say whether extra money would be made available.

MPs will debate the health budget, which covers Veilig Thuis, on Wednesday and Thursday.

If you have experienced or are experiencing domestic or sexual violence, Veilig Thuis (Safe at Home) offers confidential advice 24 hours a day on 0800 2000 or at veiligthuis.nl. In an emergency, call 112.

item.title: Man, 20, arrested on suspicion of planning terrorist attack
item.description:
Man, 20, arrested on suspicion of planning terrorist attack

October 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 20-year-old man has been arrested in Capelle aan den IJssel on suspicion of planning a terrorist attack, the prosecution service has confirmed.

Police found a sword, two knives and an air pistol at the man’s home when they went to investigate reports that he had been talking about his plans to use them for an attack with “as many victims as possible”.

The man was arrested on October 5, but details were only released today.

He appeared in court last Friday, October 9, where a judge ordered him to be detained for a further 14 days. Police are carrying out further inquiries.

item.title: Biotech industry calls for €450m investment in food innovation
item.description:
Biotech industry calls for €450m investment in food innovation

October 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The agriculture sector has called on the government to invest €450 million in food technology to maintain the Netherlands’ status as a world leader.

Biotech companies and research institutions such as Wageningen university say €1 billion is needed by 2040 for plant breeding and innovation, partly to deal with the challenges of climate change.

Some 50 companies and research institutions petitioned economic affairs minister Heleen Herbert and junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens to allocate more funding to the sector in a meeting at Wageningen this week.

Sjoujke Heimovaara, president of the executive board at Wageningen University and Research, said the industry needed its own equivalent of Project Beethoven, the government-back scheme to invest €2.5 billion in the Eindhoven region to support major technology companies such as ASML.

“Crops need to be constantly bred to withstand new diseases, higher temperatures because of climate change and the higher salt content in ground water,” she told the Telegraaf.

“We are still a world leader in this area, but if we don’t take action we will soon be selling our seeds and machines for harvesting these crops in China.”

Heimovaara said investing public money in facilities for the agriculture industry was justified by the wider economic benefits. “It is basic infrastructure,” she said. “You wouldn’t ask Albert Heijn to pay separately for using the motorways.”

Erkens tempered expectations that the cabinet could find €450 million for the sector, but he said there could be opportunities to use existing subsidies for food innovation.

“For example, money has been set reserved to limit the use of crop protection measures,” he said. “We could use some of that for these purposes.”

item.title: Albert Heijn and sister chains abroad hit by likely cyberattack
item.description:
Albert Heijn and sister chains abroad hit by likely cyberattack

October 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Cybersecurity experts say it is very likely someone broke into Albert Heijn’s IT systems, as the outage at the Netherlands’ biggest supermarket chain leaves empty shelves in its stores.

Albert Heijn and its parent company Ahold Delhaize have kept systems switched off since Sunday afternoon and still describe the problem only as a “cybersecurity incident”. “An organisation that big doesn’t take measures like this lightly,” cybersecurity expert Joey Fennis told broadcaster NOS.

Fennis said that if attackers had got in, they may also have viewed or stolen data. Pim Takkenberg told current affairs programme Nieuwsuur it seemed “fairly clear” that someone malicious had been in the system. “An outage doesn’t usually last this long,” he said.

A third expert, Eward Driehuis, said the chain may instead have found a weakness it could not fix quickly, and shut its systems down as a precaution. Albert Heijn says its investigation is ongoing and has not said when services will be restored.

Supply chain
Albert Heijn has six distribution centres in the Netherlands. CEO Margaret Versteden-van Duijn told NOS on Monday that work at some of them had stopped completely, but she would not say which ones.

According to an email to suppliers seen by RTL Z, only the Zaandam centre is still operating, and suppliers have been asked to deliver there alone, in agreed time slots. Albert Heijn has not confirmed this.

The chain says fruit, vegetables and other fresh produce will be hardest to find, while frozen goods, bread and long-life products should remain more widely available. “Of course shelves will empty if this goes on longer,” Versteden-van Duijn told NOS. “That will vary from store to store.”

Beyond the Netherlands
Belgian supermarket chain Delhaize, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, has reported IT problems. Albert Heijn’s stores in Belgium, which are supplied from the Tilburg distribution centre, may run short of some products, broadcaster VRT reported, although the chain says the impact there is limited so far.

In the US, the websites of all five Ahold Delhaize supermarket chains, including Stop & Shop and Food Lion, were offline on Monday, according to trade publication Grocery Dive. Online ordering and deliveries were also suspended, Supermarket News reported.

The incident came on the same weekend as a separate cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets in France. There, hackers remotely forced refrigeration systems to defrost, and chains including Intermarché and Coopérative U had to throw away fresh and frozen food. The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation.

The French attack targeted refrigeration equipment supplied by Danish firm Danfoss. Albert Heijn’s CEO told NOS she could not say whether the two incidents were linked, but an Ahold Delhaize spokesperson later told the news agency Reuters there was no reason to see a connection.

item.title: Dutch economy set to grow by 1.5% in 2026 as IMF raises forecast
item.description:
Dutch economy set to grow by 1.5% in 2026 as IMF raises forecast

October 13, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has improved its forecast for the Dutch economy, but warned that high prices will continue to cause pain for consumers.

The Netherlands’ GDP is now expected to grow by 1.5% this year, up from 1% in the IMF’s last assessment in July. The trend is set to continue into 2027, when the IMF expects growth of 1.3%.

The organisation says the Dutch economy will benefit from stronger than expected growth in Germany, where it has revised its prediction from 0.7% to 1.3% for this year, as well as large global investments in AI technology.

Consumer prices will grow by 2.9% this year, reflecting the high cost of energy and fuel. The statistics agency CBS reported on Tuesday that inflation had risen to 3.4% in September, continuing an upward trend that started in July.

Fuel prices have risen by 27.2% in the last year, with a litre of diesel costing nearly €2.50 at the pumps. But prices for other commodities have fallen, such as food, which is down by 1.9%.

The IMF said the impact of the conflict in Iran on fuel prices had been tempered by countries finding alternative suppliers of oil and gas.

item.title: Two-thirds of women in NL feel unheard by healthcare workers
item.description:
Two-thirds of women in NL feel unheard by healthcare workers

October 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two-thirds of women in the Netherlands say they don’t always feel heard by healthcare professionals, for example when describing symptoms, asking for referrals or discussing treatment options, according to a new report by polling company Kieskompas.

The findings were sent to MPs today and drawn from a survey of 14,000 women aged 16 and over. Only one in five women in the survey said healthcare professionals listen well to women.

Women aged 25 to 54 and women with unexplained symptoms were the most likely to say they felt misunderstood by consultants, and fewer than half of women with a condition or disability said the care they received helped them sufficiently.

Women also said they felt less well informed about topics that only affect women, such as menopause, than about general health issues. Women of all ages said they wanted that information, and would like to see more research on it.

According to ZonMw, a research funding body behind the report, girls would like to know more about how hormones can impact mental health for example.

Nearly two in three women said they thought women did not feel comfortable discussing health problems at work. Of women with health problems, 63% said these had affected their work, mainly through stress and lower productivity, and over a quarter had stopped working earlier than planned.

A second report, also presented on Monday, analysed the experiences of women who have got stuck in the healthcare system because of long-term, unexplained symptoms. The analysis, carried out by health research institute Nivel for the Voices for Women foundation, was based on surveys and accounts that women submitted themselves, which the researchers note it is not representative.

A lack of recognition came up in almost every account, ANP reported, and only one in four women said they felt heard by their care provider. According to ZonMw, almost 90% did not feel taken seriously, and 65% said they often got a psychological diagnosis when they came in with a physical complaint.

“The two new reports underline the urgency of the message ZonMw and others have been spreading for some time: more attention for women’s health is needed,” ZonMw said in a statement.

item.title: Two NSC MPs join exodus as Keijzer triggers conference walkout
item.description:
Two NSC MPs join exodus as Keijzer triggers conference walkout

October 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two former MPs for New Social Contract have resigned in protest at the party’s decision to invite right-wing independent MP Mona Keijzer to a weekend conference.

Harm Holman, NSC’s former agriculture spokesman, and Ilse Saris, who covered social affairs, said they no longer felt at home in a party that was drifting towards right-wing populism.

Saturday’s general meeting in Breda ended in chaos when the party’s entire management board resigned following a mass walkout when Keijzer stepped up onto the stage. Acting chairman Ronald de Bruin said the situation had become “untenable” after around half the delegates left the room.

Keijzer had been invited to discuss her hardline conservative movement, Project 2029, which she launched after breaking from the farmers’ party BBB earlier this year.

Holman told TV late night news show Nieuwsuur: “NSC was a reasonable centre party in terms of its policies, but it has becoming a populist party that is moving further to the right. I don’t feel at home there.”

Saris said in a parting note: “In my eyes the party has completely departed from what NSC stood for.”

Een walk-out bij het NSC-congres het moment dat @MonaKeijzer het woord neemt. Vooraf was er al veel consternatie over Keijzer als gastspreker. Het was voor @DirkGotink reden om uit de partij te stappen. Nu loopt de helft de zaal uit https://t.co/4PD2YoYwfn

— Nouschka van der Meijden (@NouschkavdM) October 10, 2026

The decision by NSC’s management  board to invite Keijzer as a guest speaker prompted its last elected parliamentarian, MEP Dirk Gotink, to resign his membership.

Gotink, 45, said in a post on LinkedIn that seeking closer ties with Keijzer was “incomprehensible”, despite the NSC leadership insisting that there was no agreement to work with her.

Voters return to CDA

NSC won 20 seats in the November 2023 election, just three months after being founded by Omtzigt, who recruited many of his candidates from his old party, the Christian Democrats (CDA).

But the party’s support collapsed soon after Omtzigt joined the right-wing coalition with Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV, the right-wing liberal VVD and the BBB the following year.

Wilders blamed NSC for blocking his plans to introduce the “harshest immigration policy ever”, while Omtzigt resigned first as party leader and then as an MP, citing the toll on his health and family life.

Many of NSC’s voters reverted to the CDA at the election last October, while NSC itself was wiped out. Holman, 69, also said at the weekend that he had rejoined the Christian Democrats.

item.title: One-way traffic on IJssel river lifted but “drought is not over”
item.description:
One-way traffic on IJssel river lifted but “drought is not over”

October 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The highways agency Rijkswaterstaat has lifted restrictions on the IJssel river that forced ships carrying freight from Arnhem to Zutphen to take a 300km detour.

A one-way system was imposed on September 24 after the river level dropped as a result of the summer drought both in the Netherlands and further upstream in Germany and Switzerland.

The agency said it was able to allow ships to travel in both directions now that the water level has risen to 1.45m above its baseline, but it warned that the drought period is “not over”.

Koninklijke Binnnenvaart Nederland, which represents inland waterway users, said the ending of the restriction was welcome, but shipping operators were still having to contend with limitations such as transporting lighter loads.

“The problems are not over. Low water is still having a big impact on inland shipping,” a spokesman said.

item.title: “Many Dutch adults can only swim one stroke”
item.description:
“Many Dutch adults can only swim one stroke”

October 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Former junior Romanian swimming champion Vlad Pațurcă moved to the Netherlands alone at the age of 21. Since then he’s founded his own swimming school in Amsterdam-Noord, where he now coaches hundreds of people. He idolises former Dutch Olympic swimming champions and dreams of one day building a squad of competitive swimmers.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?
I was a competitive swimmer in Romania, a freestyle sprinter, and swam for the youth national team. In 2021 I visited the Netherlands for the first time. The first city I saw wasn’t Amsterdam but Assen, in the north, and I fell for the Dutch way of life straight away: the quiet, the order, the way everything seemed designed for people. After that I didn’t want to be anywhere else.

I moved here at 21, with little work experience and no idea how Dutch law or business worked, and started coaching at a large adult swim club. In my first months there I saw how many adults wanted lessons. In 2024 I opened my own swim school, Win and Swim, in Amsterdam-Noord.

I paid for the first pool lane out of my own pocket and started with five or six swimmers. Since then we’ve taught more than 300 adults.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?
An international. The Netherlands is home now. Many of the people I teach are internationals too, often adults learning to swim from scratch.

How long do you plan to stay?
For good. I’ve built my business here and the plan is to grow it: more hours and new locations in Amsterdam first, then children’s lessons and other Dutch cities.
My dream is a performance squad, where I train competitive swimmers. Besides the swim school, I help companies with AI solutions.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?
Not yet, and that’s a real challenge when you run a business. So far I’ve run Win and Swim almost entirely in English, and I’m learning Dutch now so I can take the business further.

In my first years here I did A1 through a free government course while I was living in Almere. After I moved to Amsterdam I wanted to continue with A2, but the free places go first to newcomers who need the lessons to integrate, for example to find work. I was already working and settled here, so I wasn’t in that group.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?
My favourite thing is that things just work. When I opened my company, I entered my details online at the KVK chamber of commerce, went in the next day to sign and that was it: the company was open.

In Romania I’d have been running from one office to another, printing and signing papers. Here, sorting something out at the bank or the council is just as easy.

How Dutch have you become?
Dutch enough to appreciate the directness. People had told me the Dutch are cold. They’re not cold, just very direct, and at first that felt harsh. Now I value that nobody beats around the bush and nobody makes promises they don’t keep.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?
Pieter van den Hoogenband, Inge de Bruijn and Maarten van der Weijden. The first two are freestyle sprint legends, and sprint freestyle was my event. Van der Weijden came back from leukaemia to win Olympic open-water gold in 2008.

What’s your top tourist tip?
In summer, swim outdoors, but only at an official swimming spot (zwemlocatie), where the water quality is checked. Het Twiske, just north of Amsterdam-Noord, is a good one. And get on a bike. Here people of every age and every job cycle every day, and it’s the best way to see the country.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.
Almost everyone here learned to swim as a child: around 94% of Dutch youngsters hold at least one swimming diploma. You’d expect a country of strong swimmers, but the reality is more nuanced. Many Dutch adults can only swim one stroke, breaststroke with the head out of the water.

The system teaches survival rather than swimming as a sport, which makes sense in a country full of canals. As a result, many Dutch adults come back to lessons later to learn freestyle and the other strokes.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?
Spend the day on my bike, out of the city, and end it with one last swim.

Vlad was speaking with Louis Gore-Langton
